name: Security core vocabulary
description: The 100 terms a security professional needs to know, from junior analyst to CISO.

cards.subject: confidentiality
says: means information is seen only by those allowed to see it
is protected by access control and encryption
cards.use: need to stop sensitive information being read by the wrong people
not: means information stays correct and unaltered

cards.subject: integrity
says: means information stays accurate and is not changed without permission
is protected by hashing, signatures and change controls
cards.use: need to know a record has not been tampered with
not: means information is kept secret from outsiders

cards.subject: availability
says: means systems and data can be used when they are needed
is protected by redundancy, backups and defence against denial of service
cards.use: need a service to keep working when users need it
not: means information is hidden from unauthorised people

cards.subject: threat
says: is anything that could cause harm to a system or its data
may be a person, a malicious program or a natural event
cards.use: need to name something that could damage the organisation's assets
not: is a weakness in a system that can be exploited

cards.subject: vulnerability
says: is a weakness that could be used to harm a system
can be a flaw in software, a misconfiguration or a gap in process
cards.use: find an unpatched server that an attacker could use
not: is the person or group who carries out an attack

cards.subject: exploit
says: is a method or piece of code that takes advantage of a vulnerability
turns a weakness into an actual compromise
cards.use: need to name the code that takes advantage of a known flaw
not: is the weakness itself that is waiting to be used

cards.subject: attack surface
says: is the sum of the points where an attacker could try to get in
grows with every exposed service, account and interface
cards.use: need to count everything an attacker could reach
not: is the part of a system that has been fully patched

cards.subject: threat actor
says: is a person or group that carries out or intends to carry out an attack
may be a criminal gang, a state, an activist or an insider
cards.use: need to describe who might attack the organisation
not: is a weakness that can be exploited

cards.subject: security control
says: is a safeguard that prevents, detects or reduces a security risk
can be technical, physical or procedural
cards.use: need to name a measure that reduces a risk
not: is the likelihood that an attack will succeed

cards.subject: residual risk
says: is the risk that remains after controls have been applied
is accepted, transferred or reduced further
cards.use: need to say what risk is left after the safeguards are in place
not: is the risk that exists before any control is applied

cards.subject: multi-factor authentication
says: requires two or more different kinds of proof of identity
combines something you know, have or are
cards.use: want a stolen password alone to be useless to an attacker
not: uses two passwords of the same kind

cards.subject: single sign-on
says: lets a person sign in once to reach many applications
relies on an identity provider that vouches for the user
cards.use: want people to log in once rather than separately to each app
not: gives every user the same shared password

cards.subject: role-based access control
says: grants permissions according to a person's role
avoids assigning rights one person at a time
cards.use: need access to follow a job role, such as finance clerk
not: gives every user the same access

cards.subject: privileged access management
says: controls, records and limits the use of administrator accounts
can grant high-level access only for a short time
cards.use: need admin rights granted for a short time and recorded
not: gives all staff administrator rights by default

cards.subject: least privilege
says: gives each user or system only the access it needs
limits the damage if an account is compromised
cards.use: need to decide how much access a new account should have
not: gives every administrator full access to everything

cards.subject: access review
says: checks regularly that people still need the access they hold
removes rights that are no longer justified
cards.use: need to find access left over from people who changed roles
not: is the first sign-in of a new user

cards.subject: service account
says: is a non-human identity used by an application or process
often has long-lived credentials that need careful control
cards.use: need an application to log in to another system
not: is a personal login for a named employee

cards.subject: passkey
says: replaces a password with a cryptographic key pair kept on a device
resists phishing because the key works only for the real site
cards.use: want sign-in that cannot be phished into giving away a password
not: is a six-digit code sent by text message

cards.subject: session token
says: is a value that proves a user is already signed in
can be stolen and reused if it is not protected
cards.use: need to keep a user signed in between requests
not: is the password the user typed to sign in

cards.subject: identity provider
says: is the service that holds identities and confirms who a user is
issues the proof that other applications accept
cards.use: need one trusted place that confirms who users are
not: is an application that only stores files

cards.subject: firewall
says: filters network traffic according to rules
sits between networks and allows or blocks connections
cards.use: need to block unwanted connections into a network
not: scans code for flaws before it is released

cards.subject: network segmentation
says: splits a network into separate zones
limits how far an attacker can move once inside
cards.use: need a breach in one area not to reach everything
not: joins every system into one flat network

cards.subject: VPN
says: creates an encrypted tunnel across a less trusted network
lets remote users reach internal systems securely
cards.use: need staff working remotely to connect safely to the office network
not: blocks all traffic from the internet

cards.subject: DMZ
says: is a separate network zone that holds services exposed to the internet
keeps outside-facing servers apart from the internal network
cards.use: need public-facing servers kept away from internal systems
not: is a secure room for storing backups

cards.subject: intrusion detection system
says: monitors traffic or hosts and raises alerts about suspicious activity
does not itself block the activity
cards.use: want to be told about suspicious traffic without interrupting it
not: blocks suspicious traffic automatically as it passes

cards.subject: intrusion prevention system
says: inspects traffic and blocks it when it looks malicious
acts in line with the traffic it inspects
cards.use: want suspicious traffic stopped automatically
not: only records suspicious traffic and sends an alert

cards.subject: web application firewall
says: filters HTTP traffic to a web application
blocks common attacks such as injection and cross-site scripting
cards.use: need to shield a web app from common web attacks
not: filters traffic at the network level by address and port only

cards.subject: DDoS attack
says: floods a service with traffic from many sources to make it unavailable
targets availability rather than secrecy
cards.use: see a site knocked offline by a flood of requests
not: steals data by tricking users into giving up passwords

cards.subject: bastion host
says: is a hardened server that is the only way in to a private network
is closely monitored because it is exposed
cards.use: need one tightly controlled entry point to administer private servers
not: is a backup server kept offline

cards.subject: egress filtering
says: controls and monitors traffic leaving a network
can stop malware from sending data out or contacting attackers
cards.use: need to stop compromised machines talking to an attacker's server
not: blocks traffic coming in from the internet

cards.subject: OWASP Top 10
says: is a regularly updated list of the most critical web application security risks
is widely used as an awareness and training reference
cards.use: need a common list of the biggest web application risks
not: is a legal standard that every website must pass

cards.subject: SQL injection
says: inserts attacker-controlled input into a database query
is prevented by parameterised queries
cards.use: see user input joined directly into a database query
not: makes a victim's browser run attacker script

cards.subject: cross-site scripting
says: runs attacker script in another user's browser through a vulnerable page
is reduced by encoding output and a content security policy
cards.use: find user comments shown on a page without being encoded
not: changes a database query through unsafe input

cards.subject: server-side request forgery
says: tricks a server into making requests on the attacker's behalf
can reach internal services that the attacker could not reach directly
cards.use: see an app fetch any URL a user supplies, including internal ones
not: tricks a user's browser into sending a request

cards.subject: static application security testing
says: analyses source code for security flaws without running it
finds issues early in development
cards.use: want to scan code for flaws before it is run
not: tests a running application by sending it attack traffic

cards.subject: dynamic application security testing
says: tests a running application from the outside by sending attack traffic
finds flaws that appear only when the code runs
cards.use: want to test a deployed application as an attacker would
not: analyses source code without running it

cards.subject: software composition analysis
says: identifies the open-source components in an application
flags components with known vulnerabilities or risky licences
cards.use: need to know which libraries in the product have known flaws
not: tests the code you wrote for logic errors

cards.subject: threat modelling
says: works out what could go wrong with a design before it is built
identifies threats and the controls to address them
cards.use: need to find security problems in a design before any code exists
not: scans a finished application for known vulnerabilities

cards.subject: input validation
says: checks that data meets the expected rules before it is used
is a first defence against many injection attacks
cards.use: need to reject unexpected data before the application processes it
not: encrypts data before it is sent

cards.subject: security code review
says: has a person read code specifically to look for security flaws
catches issues that automated tools miss
cards.use: need a person to look for security weaknesses in a change
not: is an automated scan of a running application

cards.subject: symmetric encryption
says: uses one shared key to both encrypt and decrypt
is fast and suited to large amounts of data
cards.use: need to encrypt a large file quickly with a shared secret
not: uses a public key to encrypt and a different private key to decrypt

cards.subject: asymmetric encryption
says: uses a pair of keys, one public and one private
lets people communicate without first sharing a secret
cards.use: need to exchange data securely with someone you have never met
not: uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt

cards.subject: hash function
says: turns data of any size into a fixed-size fingerprint
cannot practically be reversed to recover the input
cards.use: need to check that data has not changed
not: scrambles data so that a key can unscramble it

cards.subject: salt
says: is random data added to a password before it is hashed
stops identical passwords producing identical hashes
cards.use: need to make precomputed password tables useless
not: is a second key used to decrypt a file

cards.subject: digital signature
says: proves who created a message and that it was not changed
is made with a private key and checked with a public key
cards.use: need to prove that a document came from a specific sender unaltered
not: is a picture of someone's handwritten name

cards.subject: public key infrastructure
says: is the set of people, policies and systems that issue and manage digital certificates
lets others trust that a public key belongs to a named owner
cards.use: need to issue and manage certificates across an organisation
not: is the infrastructure that stores only private keys

cards.subject: certificate authority
says: is a trusted body that issues digital certificates
vouches that a public key belongs to a named site or person
cards.use: need a trusted party to vouch for a website's identity
not: is a tool that scans websites for vulnerabilities

cards.subject: key rotation
says: replaces cryptographic keys regularly or after a suspected compromise
limits how much data any one key protects
cards.use: need to retire a key that has been used for a long time
not: stores keys in one place forever

cards.subject: hardware security module
says: is a tamper-resistant device that stores keys and performs cryptographic operations
keeps private keys from ever leaving the device
cards.use: need to keep the most important keys in tamper-resistant hardware
not: is a software library for encrypting files

cards.subject: perfect forward secrecy
says: uses a fresh session key for each connection
means a stolen long-term key cannot reveal past recorded sessions
cards.use: need past traffic to stay safe even if the server's key is stolen later
not: uses one key for every session

cards.subject: phishing
says: tricks people into revealing information or running malware with a fake message
often imitates a trusted sender
cards.use: receive a fake email that asks you to sign in on a copied site
not: floods a server with traffic until it fails

cards.subject: spear phishing
says: is phishing aimed at a specific person or organisation
uses personal details to look convincing
cards.use: see a message that names you and your manager and asks for an urgent payment
not: sends the same generic message to millions of people

cards.subject: ransomware
says: encrypts or locks data and demands payment to restore it
can also threaten to publish stolen data
cards.use: find files locked with a note demanding money
not: quietly records keystrokes without damaging files

cards.subject: social engineering
says: manipulates people into giving up access or information
exploits trust, urgency or fear rather than technical flaws
cards.use: hear a caller pretending to be IT and asking for a password
not: exploits a flaw in software code

cards.subject: credential stuffing
says: tries username and password pairs leaked from other breaches
works because people reuse passwords
cards.use: see many login attempts that use real leaked passwords
not: tries every possible password in order

cards.subject: man-in-the-middle attack
says: secretly sits between two parties and reads or alters their messages
is made harder by encryption and certificate checks
cards.use: worry that someone could read traffic on a public wifi network
not: floods a server from many machines

cards.subject: zero-day vulnerability
says: is a flaw unknown to the vendor so that no fix exists
can be used by attackers before defenders can patch it
cards.use: need to name a flaw that attackers are using and that has no patch
not: is a flaw that was fixed years ago

cards.subject: advanced persistent threat
says: is a well-resourced attacker that stays hidden in a network for a long time
often pursues a specific goal such as espionage
cards.use: need to name a patient, well-funded attacker targeting you over months
not: is a quick opportunistic attack by a lone amateur

cards.subject: insider threat
says: is a risk from someone with legitimate access, such as an employee or contractor
may be malicious or careless
cards.use: worry about harm from a trusted person inside the organisation
not: is a risk only from outside attackers

cards.subject: supply chain attack
says: compromises a supplier or software dependency to reach its customers
can spread through a trusted update
cards.use: see malicious code arrive in a trusted vendor's update
not: attacks an organisation directly through its own front door

cards.subject: SIEM
says: collects and correlates logs from many systems
raises alerts when events together suggest an attack
cards.use: need one place that gathers logs and alerts on suspicious patterns
not: blocks traffic at the network edge

cards.subject: security operations centre
says: is the team and facility that monitors and responds to security events
works around the clock in many organisations
cards.use: need people watching for and responding to threats
not: is the room where backups are stored

cards.subject: alert triage
says: sorts security alerts by seriousness
decides which to investigate first and which to dismiss
cards.use: face hundreds of alerts and need to decide what to look at first
not: closes every alert without review

cards.subject: false positive
says: is an alert for activity that is actually harmless
wastes analyst time when there are too many
cards.use: see a security tool flag normal behaviour as an attack
not: is a real attack that the tool failed to notice

cards.subject: indicator of compromise
says: is a piece of evidence that a system may have been breached
includes things such as a malicious file hash or IP address
cards.use: have a known bad file hash to search for across machines
not: is a weakness that could be exploited in future

cards.subject: threat intelligence
says: is information about attackers, their methods and their targets
helps defenders anticipate and spot attacks
cards.use: need to know which attackers target your industry and how
not: is a log of every login on the network

cards.subject: threat hunting
says: is proactively searching a network for attackers that alerts have missed
starts from a hypothesis about how an attacker might behave
cards.use: want to look for hidden attackers rather than wait for an alert
not: is responding to an alert as it arrives

cards.subject: endpoint detection and response
says: monitors laptops and servers for malicious behaviour
lets analysts investigate and isolate a compromised device
cards.use: need to see and contain an attack on a laptop
not: filters traffic at the network perimeter

cards.subject: SOAR
says: automates security workflows and responses
runs playbooks to enrich alerts and take action
cards.use: want routine alert handling and responses to run automatically
not: gathers logs from many systems for correlation

cards.subject: mean time to detect
says: is the average time between an attack starting and being noticed
falls as monitoring improves
cards.use: need to measure how quickly attacks are spotted
not: is the average time to recover after an attack is found

cards.subject: incident response plan
says: sets out who does what when a security incident happens
covers detection, containment, recovery and communication
cards.use: need agreed steps to follow when a breach is discovered
not: lists the risks the organisation has already accepted

cards.subject: containment
says: stops an incident from spreading
may isolate a device, disable an account or block an address
cards.use: need to stop an attack spreading while it is investigated
not: removes the attacker's tools from every system

cards.subject: eradication
says: removes the cause of an incident, such as malware and attacker access
comes after containment
cards.use: need to remove the attacker's foothold completely
not: stops the incident spreading while it is investigated

cards.subject: digital forensics
says: collects and examines digital evidence to establish what happened
is done so that the evidence stays reliable
cards.use: need to establish exactly what an attacker did
not: restores systems from backup

cards.subject: chain of custody
says: records who handled evidence and when
shows the evidence has not been altered
cards.use: need to show that evidence is trustworthy if it is used in a legal case
not: is the order in which alerts are investigated

cards.subject: playbook
says: is a step-by-step guide for handling a particular type of incident
can be partly automated
cards.use: need a ready procedure for a phishing or ransomware case
not: is the overall plan for the whole organisation's security

cards.subject: tabletop exercise
says: is a discussion-based rehearsal of how a team would handle an incident
tests plans without touching live systems
cards.use: want to practise an incident response without real systems at risk
not: is a live attack run against production systems

cards.subject: breach notification
says: is telling regulators and affected people that personal data was exposed
is often required within a set time by law
cards.use: find that customer data was exposed and the people affected must be told
not: is an internal alert that a server is down

cards.subject: root cause analysis
says: finds the underlying reason an incident happened
aims to fix the cause rather than just the symptom
cards.use: need to find why an incident happened so that it does not recur
not: restores service as quickly as possible

cards.subject: immutable backup
says: is a backup that cannot be changed or deleted for a set period
protects recovery data from ransomware
cards.use: need backups that an attacker cannot encrypt or erase
not: is a backup stored on the same server as the original

cards.subject: risk assessment
says: identifies risks and judges their likelihood and impact
ranks risks so effort goes where it matters most
cards.use: need to decide which security risks matter most
not: tests whether a system can be broken into

cards.subject: security policy
says: sets out the organisation's rules and expectations for security
applies to all staff and systems it covers
cards.use: need to state what staff must and must not do
not: is the technical setting on one firewall

cards.subject: data classification
says: labels data by how sensitive it is
decides how each label must be handled and protected
cards.use: need to decide how carefully a document must be handled
not: encrypts every file on a disk

cards.subject: acceptable use policy
says: tells staff what they may and may not do with company systems
is usually agreed when someone joins
cards.use: need to tell staff how they may use work devices and accounts
not: sets the technical rules for a firewall

cards.subject: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
says: organises security activity into functions such as identify, protect, detect, respond and recover
is a voluntary framework from a US standards body
cards.use: need a common structure to describe and improve security
not: is a certification awarded by a UK scheme

cards.subject: Cyber Essentials
says: is a UK scheme that certifies a set of basic technical controls
covers things like firewalls, patching and access control
cards.use: need a basic UK certification for core security controls
not: is a payment card industry standard

cards.subject: PCI DSS
says: is a standard for organisations that handle payment card data
sets requirements for protecting cardholder information
cards.use: need to protect and handle card payments correctly
not: is a framework that organises security into five functions

cards.subject: third-party risk assessment
says: evaluates the security risks of a supplier before and during a relationship
may use questionnaires, evidence and audits
cards.use: need to judge whether a supplier is safe to give access to your data
not: tests your own network for weaknesses

cards.subject: security audit
says: is a formal review of whether security controls and policies are followed
produces findings that need fixing
cards.use: need an independent check of whether security rules are followed
not: is a simulated attack by a hired team

cards.subject: security awareness training
says: teaches staff to recognise and report security threats
includes things like spotting phishing messages
cards.use: want staff to spot phishing and report it
not: is a technical control that blocks malware

cards.subject: vulnerability scan
says: is an automated check of systems for known weaknesses
produces a list of findings to fix
cards.use: need a regular automated check for known flaws
not: is a person manually trying to break in

cards.subject: patch management
says: is the process of testing and installing software updates
closes known vulnerabilities
cards.use: need to make sure known flaws are fixed promptly
not: is a scan that finds weaknesses

cards.subject: CVE
says: is a public identifier for a specific known vulnerability
lets everyone refer to the same flaw
cards.use: need a standard name for a published vulnerability
not: is a score for how severe a flaw is

cards.subject: CVSS
says: is a standard scoring system for the severity of vulnerabilities
gives a score from zero to ten
cards.use: need a standard measure of how serious a vulnerability is
not: is the public identifier assigned to a vulnerability

cards.subject: red team
says: is a group that simulates a real attacker to test defences
tests people and processes as well as technology
cards.use: want to test whether the organisation could detect and stop a realistic attack
not: is the group that defends systems from attack

cards.subject: blue team
says: is the group that defends systems and responds to attacks
monitors, detects and recovers
cards.use: need to name the defenders in an exercise
not: is the group that simulates an attacker

cards.subject: bug bounty programme
says: invites outside researchers to report vulnerabilities for a reward
pays for valid findings
cards.use: want outside researchers to report flaws responsibly for a reward
not: is a paid internal team that scans every system

cards.subject: security champion
says: is someone in a delivery team who promotes security practices
links the team to the security function
cards.use: want security knowledge inside each product team
not: is the most senior security executive

cards.subject: DevSecOps
says: builds security into the development and operations pipeline
automates security checks alongside testing
cards.use: want security checks to run automatically in the delivery pipeline
not: adds a security review only after release

cards.subject: shift left
says: moves security work earlier in the development lifecycle
finds problems when they are cheapest to fix
cards.use: want design and code flaws found before testing or release
not: delays security checks until just before launch

qa.q: Which part of the CIA triad means that information is seen only by people allowed to see it?
qa.why: Confidentiality is about keeping information from unauthorised people.

qa.q: You get an email asking you to sign in through a link to keep your account. What attack could this be?
qa.why: Phishing uses a fake message to get people to give up information.

qa.q: A caller says they are from IT and asks for your password to fix a problem. What is this?
qa.why: It manipulates a person rather than a system.

qa.q: What does multi-factor authentication require?
qa.right: Two or more different kinds of proof of identity
qa.why: The factors must be of different kinds, such as a password and a device.

qa.q: All your files are locked and a note demands payment to open them. What is this?
qa.why: Ransomware locks data and demands payment.

qa.q: Which document tells staff what they may and may not do with work laptops and accounts?
qa.why: An acceptable use policy sets out permitted use.

qa.q: You receive a suspicious email. What should you do?
qa.right: Report it through the agreed route and do not click anything
wrong: Forward it to colleagues to ask what they think
Reply and ask the sender if it is real
qa.why: Reporting lets the security team protect others too.

qa.q: What does a firewall do?
qa.right: Filters network traffic according to rules
wrong: Encrypts every file on a disk
qa.why: A firewall allows or blocks connections.

qa.q: Which team monitors and responds to security events around the clock?
qa.why: A SOC watches for and responds to threats.

qa.q: A website is knocked offline by a flood of requests from many machines. Which part of the CIA triad was attacked?
qa.why: A DDoS attack stops people using a service.

qa.q: A new intern needs to read one shared folder. What should you grant?
qa.right: Read access to that folder only
wrong: The same access as their manager
Read access to every folder in case they need it
qa.why: Least privilege gives only the access needed.

qa.q: How should a system store users' passwords?
wrong: Encrypted with a key kept in the same database
In plain text, protected by the firewall
qa.why: Hashing with a salt cannot practically be reversed.

qa.q: Code that takes advantage of a published flaw is called what?
qa.why: An exploit turns a weakness into a compromise.

qa.q: A tool alerts on your normal nightly backup as if it were an attack. What is this?
qa.why: A false positive is an alert for harmless activity.

qa.q: Which concept decides how carefully a document must be handled, based on how sensitive it is?
qa.why: Classification labels data and sets how it must be handled.

qa.q: An email names you and your manager and asks for an urgent payment. What is it likely to be?
qa.why: Spear phishing is aimed at a specific person using personal details.

qa.q: Remote staff need to reach internal systems safely over the internet. What do you provide?
qa.why: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel.

qa.q: A search page builds its database query by joining in user text. What is the fix?
qa.why: Parameterised queries prevent SQL injection.

qa.q: A comment containing a script runs in other visitors' browsers. What is the flaw?
qa.why: Unencoded output lets attacker script run.

qa.q: How can you reduce the risk of someone reading your traffic on public wifi?
qa.right: Use encrypted connections such as HTTPS or a VPN
wrong: Connect to every open network to find the best one
qa.why: Encryption stops a man in the middle reading the data.

qa.q: Many login attempts use real passwords leaked from another company's breach. What helps most?
qa.why: Credential stuffing works because passwords are reused.

qa.q: Which tool blocks suspicious traffic automatically as it passes?
qa.why: A prevention system acts in line with the traffic.

qa.q: A laptop is infected and spreading malware. What is the first step?
qa.right: Contain it by isolating it from the network
wrong: Wipe and reinstall it straight away
Keep using it so you can watch it
Email everyone to warn them from it
qa.why: Containment stops the spread while evidence is kept.

qa.q: You need to isolate a compromised laptop remotely and investigate what it did. Which tool helps?
qa.why: EDR monitors and can isolate endpoints.

qa.q: A breach on the guest wifi must not be able to reach the finance servers. What do you use?
qa.why: Segmentation limits movement between zones.

qa.q: A contractor left six months ago but still has access to a system. Which practice would have found this?
qa.why: Access reviews remove rights that are no longer justified.

qa.q: An engineer with legitimate access copies customer data to take to a competitor. What kind of threat is this?
qa.why: An insider already has legitimate access.

qa.q: Which tool proves that a document came from a specific sender and was not altered?
qa.why: A signature uses a private key to prove origin and integrity.

qa.q: Which scheme gives a basic UK certification for core technical security controls?
qa.why: Cyber Essentials is the UK basic certification scheme.

qa.q: You want security checks to run automatically each time code is built. Which approach fits?
qa.why: DevSecOps builds checks into the pipeline.

qa.q: An application fetches any URL a user gives it, and an attacker uses it to reach an internal metadata service. What is the flaw?
qa.why: The server is tricked into making requests for the attacker.

qa.q: You want to scan source code for flaws in the build pipeline before anything is run. Which testing is this?
qa.why: Static testing examines code without running it.

qa.q: Which analysis finds known vulnerabilities in the open-source libraries you use?
qa.why: It identifies components and their known flaws.

qa.q: A malicious update arrives from a trusted vendor and spreads to its customers. What is this attack?
qa.why: Attackers compromised a supplier to reach customers.

qa.q: After isolating an infected server you remove the malware and the attacker's access. What stage is this?
qa.why: Eradication removes the cause after containment.

qa.q: Customer personal data has been exposed. What is the legal duty?
qa.right: Notify the regulator and affected people within the time the law requires
wrong: Wait to see if anyone notices
qa.why: Breach notification is often time-limited.

qa.q: Attackers encrypt your servers and try to delete your backups. Which backup protection helps?
wrong: Backups kept only on a laptop
Weekly backups that overwrite the last one
qa.why: Immutable backups cannot be changed or deleted for a period.

qa.q: You need admin rights granted for two hours and the actions recorded. What do you use?
qa.why: PAM controls, records and limits admin use.

qa.q: A private key may have been exposed. What should you do?
qa.right: Replace it by rotating the key
wrong: Keep it, since nothing has happened
Hash it and keep using it
qa.why: Key rotation replaces a possibly compromised key.

qa.q: The team rehearses a ransomware incident by talking it through, without touching live systems. What is this?
qa.why: A tabletop is a discussion-based rehearsal.

qa.q: You handle card payments and need to know which standard applies. Which is it?
qa.why: PCI DSS covers payment card data.

qa.q: After you add controls, some risk remains. What is it called?
qa.why: Residual risk is what is left after controls.

qa.q: You hire a team to simulate a realistic attacker and see whether you detect it. What is this?
qa.why: A red team tests defences as a real attacker would.

qa.q: Before giving a supplier access to customer data, you check their security. What is this called?
wrong: A penetration test of your network
qa.why: It evaluates a supplier's risks.

qa.q: Attacks are on average noticed 80 days after they begin. Which measure shows this?
qa.why: It measures how quickly attacks are spotted.

qa.q: Your analysts go looking for hidden attackers without waiting for an alert. What is this?
qa.why: Threat hunting is proactive.

qa.q: Malware on a server keeps contacting an attacker's address. Which control could stop the data leaving?
qa.why: Egress filtering controls outbound traffic.

qa.q: A server's long-term key is stolen, but past recorded sessions stay safe. Which property is this?
qa.why: Each session uses a fresh key.

qa.q: You need to keep the most important keys in tamper-resistant hardware. What do you use?
qa.why: An HSM keeps keys inside tamper-resistant hardware.

qa.q: You want routine alert handling to run automatically through playbooks. What do you use?
qa.why: SOAR automates workflows and responses.

qa.q: Evidence from a laptop may be used in court. What record shows it was not altered?
qa.why: It records who handled the evidence and when.

qa.q: A team wants design flaws found before any code is written. Which principle fits?
qa.right: Shift left, with threat modelling at design time
wrong: Do a penetration test after release
Wait for a bug bounty report
qa.why: Shifting left finds problems when they are cheapest to fix.

qa.q: A critical flaw has no vendor patch and is being used in attacks. What is it?
wrong: A known exploit with a patch
qa.why: A zero-day has no fix when attackers use it.

qa.q: A new public-facing server must sit apart from the internal network. What design places it?
wrong: A VPN endpoint on the finance network
qa.why: A DMZ holds services exposed to the internet.
